newsitem.title: USA: ALPINE SKIING-SCHIFFERER WINS RACE, ALPHAND GETS SUPER-G TITLE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SCHIFFERER WINS RACE, ALPHAND GETS SUPER-G TITLE.

text.p: Austrian Andreas Schifferer continued his late-season surge by edging compatriot Josef Strobl to win the World Cup Finals Super-G on Thursday in a result that gave the season title to France's Luc Alphand.
Schifferer, who took world championship bronze in the giant slalom at Sestriere, scored his first career World Cup victory, but in so doing deprived Strobl of the Super-G crown.
"Strobl had a great chance to win the title if I finished out of the top eight," said Alphand, who began the race with a 69-point lead. "Schifferer helped me a lot today. I should buy him a beer."
The 22-year-old Schifferer squeezed ahead of Strobl by clocking a time of one minute, 33.76 seconds through the wind on Vail Mountain.
Kristian Ghedina of Italy finished third in 1:33.88, .041 of a second ahead of compatriot Luca Cattaneo.
Victory for Strobl would have lifted him past Alphand, who straggled home in ninth place to match his disappointing result in Wednesday's downhill.

Instead, Alphand emerged with the crystal globe on 351 points, while Strobl settled for second place, 18 points behind. Schifferer surged into third in the final standings ahead of compatriot Hermann Maier.

"I'm so sorry for Strobl, but one day it will probably work out the other way around," said Schifferer, who posted second-place finishes in the Super-G at Kvitjell, Norway and in the giant slalom at Shiga Kogen, Japan -- results that along with Thursday's win catapulted him to seventh place in the overall World Cup standings.
Said the 23-year-old Strobl: "It's my own fault. I knew at the start that I had to risk it all. Andy was better than I was."
Alphand, who earlier this season clinched his third successive downhill title, completed his sweep of the speed events but saw his lead in the overall standings dwindle.
Andre Kjetil Aamodt of Norway finished fifth to draw closer in his challenge to Alphand. Aamodt, the 1994 overall winner, made up 16 points to trail Alphand by 106.
Aamodt, however, has two more races to run -- Saturday's giant slalom and Sunday's slalom -- while speed specialist Alphand is through for the season.
"He has done a good job this year. Now he just has to sit back and watch. It's me who has the hard work now," said Aamodt.
"I don't feel so good about my form in the slalom but I think I have a chance to win the giant if I have a good run."
Alphand, who blamed windy conditions for his sluggishness at the bottom of the Super-G course, said he was disappointed at first to lose ground to Aamodt but then put his season in perspective.

"The ball is now in Aamodt's court," said Alphand, who is trying to become the first Frenchman since the great Jean-Claude Killy in 1968 to win the overall and the first speed specialist ever to take the biggest World Cup prize.
"At first I was disappointed but then I was completely satisfied," said the 31-year-old Frenchman, who has hinted this would be his last season of racing.
"I raced in two events and won both. I could not ask for anything more. The overall would be like the cherry on top of the cake. The results of the season have been wonderful."
